correctness.rationale: For a>b>0, N>=2 and 1<=n<N the inverse-square ellipsoid matrix equals beta I-(beta-alpha)e1 e1^T with alpha=a^-2, beta=b^-2. Its subspace compression has smallest eigenvalue alpha+(beta-alpha)T, where T is the squared projection onto the n-dimensional complement. Rotational invariance and the Gaussian chi-square representation give T~Beta(n/2,(N-n)/2), including N-n=1. Monotone inversion proves the stated complete CDF and factor-C success curve; Euler's beta integral proves all q>0 moments. The infimum section radius is b, attained by subspaces of e1-perp. The high-anisotropy formula (T+(1-T)/kappa^2)^(-1/2) and beta variance 2n(N-n)/(N^2(N+2)) prove both limits. Independent bounded projection and moment comparisons corroborate, but do not establish, the universal proof.

originality.rationale: The closest 2026 study explicitly treats two-valued semiaxis sequences, including m=1, but its Section 6.3 Propositions 6.12-6.14 give probability bounds rather than the exact finite beta pushforward and its complete CDF/moments. The 2021 Hilbert-ellipsoid paper supplies general random-radius inequalities and, in Lemma 25, the same elementary Haar projection statistic for an auxiliary coordinate-recovery problem; it does not present the full one-spike radius law. The exact specialization uses standard rank-one spectral algebra and the classical beta law and is therefore modest, vulnerable to prior folklore, and not a new general random-section bound.
residual_risks: An older random-matrix, multivariate statistics or stochastic geometry treatment could state the exact rank-one compressed eigenvalue law under another name.
The derivation is short from standard spectral algebra and Haar beta projection. Its mathematical novelty is the natural exact geometric specialization, not a new general technique.

value.rationale: A centered ellipsoid with one outlying semiaxis is the minimal anisotropic test of random-versus-optimal information. The exact finite CDF, positive moments and factor-C success curve supply a reusable calibration for sharpness questions, while the proportional-codimension limit realizes the precise sqrt(N/n) scale. Prior broad inequalities do not provide those exact probabilities. This is a narrowly scoped elementary exact benchmark, not a general improvement for arbitrary ellipsoids.

limitations: Only centered one-spike real Euclidean ellipsoids; N>=2 and 1<=n<N; exact radial law but no full section spectrum for multi-level ellipsoids.
Haar projection beta law and rank-one compression are standard constituent facts; possibility of prior equivalent compilation remains.
